title: Laredo Aggie Moms turn Howdy spirit into scholarships — and the next fundraiser is bowling for books
excerpt: The Laredo Texas A&M Mothers' Club welcomed a record-setting crowd at its Howdy Party, honored this year's scholarship recipients, and is now gearing up its 2nd Annual Bowling Tournament.
content:
Some of the best news in Laredo this fall does not come from a council chamber or a courtroom. It comes from a room full of mothers in maroon, raising money so Webb County students can afford to become Aggies.

The Laredo Texas A&M Mothers' Club drew one of its largest turnouts in recent years at its annual Howdy Party and Membership Drive, held July 23 at the IBC Annex on Jacaman Road. The evening, sponsored by Commerce Bank, brought together incoming Aggies, current students, parents, alumni and community members — and recognized this year's scholarship recipients, whose academic achievements the club says exemplify the Aggie spirit.

The night opened with a practical gift: a financial presentation from Commerce Bank representatives on budgeting, managing personal finances, and protecting against financial scams — tools for families sending a student off to College Station. Club President Sheri Porras, who leads the club for 2026–2027, then welcomed families and laid out the club's mission: supporting the comfort, welfare and success of Aggie students while raising funds for deserving students from Laredo and Webb County.

Guest speaker Kayla Alvarado shared her own Aggie story to encourage incoming students, and the evening paused for a tribute to J.J. Sanchez, whose life and legacy the club honors through the J.J. Sanchez Memorial Scholarship, awarded in his memory to help future Aggies reach their educational goals.

The club thanked Commerce Bank — and its president and CEO, Ignacio Urrabazo Jr. — along with the volunteers, donors and local businesses whose raffle prizes and volunteer hours made the evening possible. The celebration also welcomed the club's newest Aggie Moms into a family the club describes as lifelong support, not just a school-year commitment.

The scale behind the local party is striking. The Federation of Texas A&M University Mothers' Clubs, founded in 1928, counts 110 clubs and more than 7,300 members nationwide. In the 2025–2026 year alone it awarded more than $1 million in scholarships and nearly $144,000 to student organizations — and since 2007 it has returned more than $12.1 million to Texas A&M students.

And the work is not done. The Laredo club is now gearing up for its 2nd Annual Bowling Tournament, its next scholarship fundraiser, calling on teams, sponsors, donors and raffle prizes to keep the scholarship fund growing. Its October meeting — members in pink, finances reviewed, plans ahead — set the tone: every dollar raised is a Webb County student closer to a degree.

For families weighing college costs, that is the kind of community infrastructure that matters as much as any headline: neighbors organizing, businesses sponsoring, and scholarships landing where they are needed.
